description: Bake two sourdough loaves at once from 1000 g of flour. Work out the water, starter, and salt for a double batch, with the table and freezing notes.

examples.result: Add 900 g flour, 650 g water, 200 g starter, and 20 g salt. Total dough 1770 g, two loaves of about 885 g each.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 1000 × 0.20 = 200 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 100 g of flour and 100 g of water.
Total water is 75% of the flour: 1000 × 0.75 = 750 g. Water to add is 750 - 100 = 650 g.
Flour to add is 1000 - 100 = 900 g. Salt is 2%: 1000 × 0.02 = 20 g.
examples.title: 1000 g flour at 75% hydration, two loaves

faqs.answer: 1770 g of dough: 900 g flour to add, 650 g water to add, 200 g starter, and 20 g salt. Split in half, that is two loaves of about 885 g each, which bake to roughly 830 g apiece. The Perfect Loaf's best sourdough makes two 900 g loaves from a similar batch.
faqs.question: How much dough does a two-loaf batch make?

faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the simplest way to scale. Doubling the flour doubles everything else, because baker's percentages are all relative to the flour. The only thing that does not double is the fermentation time: a bigger batch ferments a little faster, because the dough holds its own warmth, so watch it rather than the clock.
faqs.question: Is a double batch just double the single recipe?

faqs.answer: Yes. Shape both loaves, put both baskets in the fridge, and bake them one at a time straight from cold. The second loaf waits happily in the fridge while the first one bakes. If you have two Dutch ovens and an oven big enough, bake them side by side.
faqs.question: Can I bake the loaves one at a time?

faqs.answer: Slice it first, then freeze the slices in a freezer bag with the air pressed out. Frozen slices go straight into the toaster, and you thaw only what you need. Bread keeps its flavour well in the freezer for a few months if it is wrapped tight.
faqs.question: How do I freeze the second loaf?

faqs.answer: A double batch needs a bigger bowl than you think. A 1770 g dough needs room to nearly double in size, so use the largest bowl you own, or split the dough into two bowls for bulk fermentation. A dough that overflows the bowl is a mess that is hard to rescue.
faqs.question: What size bowl do I need for two loaves?

felicityNote: I bake two loaves every week now: one for the table, one sliced and frozen. The second loaf costs me about ten extra minutes, and it means we never run out.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it. Two loaves start at 1000 g.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 75%, every 100 g of flour holds 75 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 1000 g of flour takes 200 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 1000 g of flour takes 20 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %. Divide the total dough in half for two loaves.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Use your largest bowl. Weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add, holding back about 30 g of the water for now. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left. A double batch is heavy to mix by hand, so take your time and add the held-back water only if the dough wants it.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then fold every 30 minutes for the first two hours: stretch and folds early, coil folds later. A bigger batch ferments a little faster, so watch it.

howToSteps.name: Divide and shape
howToSteps.text: When the dough has risen about half as big again, turn it out and divide it in half with a bench scraper. Shape each half into a round or a loaf and basket them seam side up.

howToSteps.name: Cold proof, then bake
howToSteps.text: Cover both baskets and refrigerate overnight. Bake straight from the fridge, one at a time if you have one Dutch oven. The second loaf waits happily in the fridge.

lede: Two loaves take barely more effort than one: the same mixing, the same folds, and a second basket in the fridge. This batch is built on 1000 g of flour at 75% hydration, and it splits into two loaves of about 885 g each.

title: Sourdough Calculator: Two Loaves
tutorial: Two loaves take barely more effort than one. The mixing is the same, the folds are the same, and the only extra work is shaping a second loaf and finding room for a second basket in the fridge. If you bake every week, a double batch is the easiest way to stay ahead: one loaf for the table, one sliced and frozen for the days you do not bake.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 1000 g of total flour at 75% hydration, the dough holds 750 g of water in total. Your starter brings 100 g of that water, because 200 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 650 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 100 g of flour, so you add 900 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 20 g. The total dough is 1770 g, which splits into two loaves of about 885 g each.

The one thing that does not double is the timing. A bigger batch of dough holds its own warmth and ferments a little faster than a single loaf, so watch the dough rather than the clock. If your single loaves bulk ferment in four hours, the double batch may be ready in three and a half. The signs are the same: about half as big again, domed, and jiggly.

You need a bigger bowl than you think. A 1770 g dough needs room to nearly double in size, so use the largest bowl you own, or split the dough into two bowls for bulk fermentation. A dough that overflows the bowl is a mess that is hard to rescue, and it is the most common mistake in a first double batch.

Baking two loaves with one Dutch oven is simple: shape both, basket both, refrigerate both, and bake them one at a time straight from the fridge. The second loaf waits happily in the cold while the first one bakes. When the second loaf is cool, slice it and freeze the slices in a freezer bag with the air pressed out. Frozen slices go straight into the toaster, and you thaw only what you need.
